case_info.scenario: A man aged 44 years was referred for progressive parkinsonism with poor levodopa response. His medical history comprised unexplained sensory hearing loss, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. At age 23 years, he had bilateral cataract surgery, and over the last 2 years, he developed worsening stiffness and walking difficulties with frequent falls. He reported features of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder, restless legs syndrome (RLS), visual daytime hallucinations, and rapid cognitive decline. He was given levodopa/benserazide (up to 200 mg/50 mg 4 times daily) without improvement on his Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale scores. Therefore, his dopaminergic medication was ceased. Family history was negative for movement or developmental disorders. His neurologic examination showed hypomimia, symmetrical bradykinesia, and rigidity of the extremities without tremors (Video). There was full range of eye movements with large-amplitude saccadic intrusions on smooth pursuit in all directions. Neuropsychological assessment revealed significant abnormalities in cognitive functioning, affecting verbal and nonverbal cognitive skills (ie, speed of information processing, visuospatial skills, verbal and visual memory loss, executive skills). Mini-Mental Status Examination score was 26 of 30 points. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing (ie, paraneoplastic antibodies Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2, Ma2, amphiphysin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, N-methyl-d-aspartic acid, LGI1, and Caspr2, 14-3-3 protein) were normal. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed mild frontal and parietal atrophy. An electroencephalogram demonstrated slowing in keeping with moderate generalized encephalopathy. Total-body positron emission tomography (PET) using fluorine 18 (18F) fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) as a tracer showed no FDG-avid lesions; however, a subsequent brain-specific FDG-PET/MRI revealed hypometabolism throughout the left cerebral hemisphere and crossed cerebellar diaschisis (Figure 1). As the patient’s cognitive function and parkinsonism had deteriorated rapidly, a brain biopsy of the left frontal cortex was done. Immunohistochemistry showed scattered globular inclusions consistent with Lewy bodies.

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Neuropsychological assessment revealed significant abnormalities in cognitive functioning, affecting verbal and nonverbal cognitive skills (ie, speed of information processing, visuospatial skills, verbal and visual memory loss, executive skills). Laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing (ie, paraneoplastic antibodies Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2, Ma2, amphiphysin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, N-methyl-d-aspartic acid, LGI1, and Caspr2, 14-3-3 protein) were normal. case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{

    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{

    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.scenario: A man aged 44 years was referred for progressive parkinsonism with poor levodopa response. His medical history comprised unexplained sensory hearing loss, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. At age 23 years, he had bilateral cataract surgery, and over the last 2 years, he developed worsening stiffness and walking difficulties with frequent falls. He reported features of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder, restless legs syndrome (RLS), visual daytime hallucinations, and rapid cognitive decline. He was given levodopa/benserazide (up to 200 mg/50 mg 4 times daily) without improvement on his Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale scores. Therefore, his dopaminergic medication was ceased. Family history was negative for movement or developmental disorders. His neurologic examination showed hypomimia, symmetrical bradykinesia, and rigidity of the extremities without tremors (Video). There was full range of eye movements with large-amplitude saccadic intrusions on smooth pursuit in all directions. Neuropsychological assessment revealed significant abnormalities in cognitive functioning, affecting verbal and nonverbal cognitive skills (ie, speed of information processing, visuospatial skills, verbal and visual memory loss, executive skills). Mini-Mental Status Examination score was 26 of 30 points. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing (ie, paraneoplastic antibodies Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2, Ma2, amphiphysin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, N-methyl-d-aspartic acid, LGI1, and Caspr2, 14-3-3 protein) were normal. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed mild frontal and parietal atrophy. An electroencephalogram demonstrated slowing in keeping with moderate generalized encephalopathy. Total-body positron emission tomography (PET) using fluorine 18 (18F) fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) as a tracer showed no FDG-avid lesions; however, a subsequent brain-specific FDG-PET/MRI revealed hypometabolism throughout the left cerebral hemisphere and crossed cerebellar diaschisis (Figure 1). As the patient’s cognitive function and parkinsonism had deteriorated rapidly, a brain biopsy of the left frontal cortex was done. Immunohistochemistry showed scattered globular inclusions consistent with Lewy bodies.

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it

  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.

  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller

  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.
